Title: Scene-selective cortex encodes navigational affordances independently of visual features
Authors: Michael F. Bonner, Russell A. Epstein
Abstract: Humans rapidly perceive where they can move in a scene. We used fMRI and representational similarity analysis to test whether scene-selective regions (OPA, PPA, RSC) encode the paths available for navigation in images of indoor environments. Participants viewed 300 rendered rooms while performing an orthogonal task. Navigational affordance maps, derived from human path annotations, explained unique variance in OPA responses beyond low- and mid-level visual features and beyond a deep convolutional network trained on object recognition. A network trained to predict navigational paths better matched OPA representations. These results suggest that OPA computes affordance-based representations that support visually guided navigation.

Title: Serial dependence in orientation judgments arises at a perceptual rather than decisional stage
Authors: Mauro Manassi, David Whitney, Jason Fischer
Abstract: Perceptual judgments are biased toward recently seen stimuli, a phenomenon termed serial dependence. Whether this bias reflects altered perception or post-perceptual decision and memory processes remains debated. Across four psychophysical experiments (N = 120) we measured orientation adjustment errors for Gabor patches while manipulating response requirements, inter-trial intervals, and whether the previous stimulus required a response. We fit a Bayesian observer model with separate perceptual and decisional bias terms and recorded EEG to decode stimulus orientation over time. Attraction toward the previous orientation was present even when no response was made on the prior trial, was reflected in early decoded orientation representations (~120 ms), and was best captured by the perceptual term of the model. These findings indicate that serial dependence alters perceptual representations themselves, supporting a role for continuity fields in stabilizing visual perception.
